Whose rulings do you mainly follow (taqlid)?

part1.text: The rulings in the classical books of fiqh should be followed today as they are, unless a living marja' rules otherwise.
The Imams know the unseen, including future events, by God's permission.
If a reliable hadith seems to conflict with reason, we should accept the hadith and assume our understanding is limited.
Modern ideas such as human rights and gender equality are good reasons to look again at classical rulings.
God has given the Imams authority to act within the created world (wilaya takwiniyya).
Reason can tell us what is just and unjust, independently of revelation.
A daughter inheriting half of a son's share is a fixed ruling that should not change with social conditions.
The Imams are best understood as supremely pious, divinely guided scholars and leaders, without powers over creation.
A single reliable narrator's report is enough to establish a point of belief, not only a legal ruling.
Many classical rulings reflected the society they were made in, so their purpose matters more than their exact wording.
Calling directly on an Imam for help, as in 'Ya Ali madad', is legitimate.
Philosophy and rational theology are essential tools for understanding religion properly.
The hawza's classical method of ijtihad is enough to answer the questions modern life raises.
Many narrations describing the Imams' extraordinary powers are probably later exaggerations.
Greek-influenced philosophy and mysticism have distorted Shia teaching.
Academic research from universities, including by non-Muslim scholars, should shape how we understand our tradition.
The Imams were created as lights before the creation of the world.
A hadith that contradicts clear scientific knowledge should be reinterpreted or set aside.
Following a living marja' (taqlid) in matters of practice is essential for most believers.
Imam Husayn's journey to Karbala is best understood through its political and historical circumstances, rather than through his foreknowledge of the outcome.
The Four Books of hadith are broadly reliable as a whole.
Women should be able to become maraji' and judges.
Commemorations such as Muharram majalis and Fatimiyya are central to faith, not just cultural tradition.
Every hadith should be checked for its chain and its content before being used, even in the famous collections.
Islam already contains everything a just society needs, so we don't need to borrow ethical frameworks from outside it.
Accusations of ghuluww against some popular devotional practices are often justified.
When in doubt, it is better to follow the texts cautiously than to reason your way to a new conclusion.
Some established practices in our communities are cultural rather than religious, and should be reformed.
The Imams hear us and can respond when we visit their shrines or address them.
Islamic philosophers such as Mulla Sadra and Allama Tabataba'i deepen faith rather than threaten it.
Changes in religious rulings should come only from senior jurists, not from public debate.
Beliefs about the Imams should rest only on the Quran and on reports that give certainty, not on single narrations.
Ordinary believers can understand religion directly from the Imams' words, without specialised legal theory.
Religious knowledge develops over time as human knowledge grows.
Ziyarat al-Jami'a al-Kabira describes the Imams' station accurately and should be taken at face value.
Usul al-fiqh, the theory of jurisprudence, is necessary to derive rulings correctly.

part2.text: A woman should be able to be president of a university Ahl al-Bayt society.
A qualified jurist has the right to lead the Muslim community politically while the Imam is in occultation.
Your kind, sincere Christian neighbour, who never becomes Muslim, can still reach Paradise.
You'd happily join a Sunni congregational prayer and count it as your own.
On the night of Ashura, you'd rather be at a packed majlis with latmiyya and matam than at a quiet talk.
The ideal country would make Islamic law the law of the land.
On a long drive on your own, what are you most likely to put on?
Existence is one reality that comes in degrees, from God, who is pure existence, down to the smallest speck of dust.
Shia living in the West should be active in local politics and civic life.
If your marja's ruling and your own reading of the Quran disagreed, you'd follow the marja'.
You'd leave a family wedding before the party if there were music and mixed dancing.
The seminary should stay out of politics and focus on teaching.
You'd rather not attend a religious service at a friend's church, even for their wedding.
Your local centre starts a weekly evening class. Which one would you sign up for?
La'n, cursing the enemies of the Ahl al-Bayt, is essential to drawing close to Allah.
Some Muharram practices damage how others see Shia Islam and should be dropped.
A state should treat all citizens equally, whatever their religion.
Questions like 'What is existence?' or 'How can an unchanging God act in time?' do little to help a believer's faith.
You'd choose a Shia school for your child, even if it were academically weaker than the alternatives.
You'd be happy to learn your religion mainly from books and podcasts by lay academics.
Mut'ah, temporary marriage, is a legitimate option for young Muslims today.
Whether a woman covers her hair should be her own decision.
A Friday sermon is the right place to urge people to join a political protest.
Other religions hold real wisdom you could learn from.
You'd be happy for your child to marry a practising Sunni.
A majlis should move people to tears more than teach them facts.
In a Muslim-majority country, eating in public during the day in Ramadan should be punishable by law.
Which of these is most a part of your week?
When you face suffering, thinking hard about why a perfect God allows it strengthens your faith more than it unsettles it.
You'd encourage a talented young person to build a career in mainstream media or government.
Seminary training should count for more than a university doctorate when someone speaks about religion.
A man taking a second wife is acceptable today, as long as he treats both wives justly.
Political movements that use the Imams' names often end up harming religion.
Only one religious path is fully true; the others are mistaken.
Where do you get most of your religious learning?
options: Majalis and talks at the centre

part2.text: Shia and Sunni scholars should work together on shared causes and play down their differences.
Money spent on lavish commemorations would do more good given to charity.
Faith is stronger when it is chosen freely than when the state enforces it.
Saying the world is a manifestation of God's names goes too far: it's safer to say only that God created it.
Close friendships with non-Muslims tend to weaken faith.
Ordinary believers should be encouraged to read Quran commentaries and form their own understanding.
Which journey would you most like to make next?
You question the existence of God.
Ashura is first of all a call to stand against injustice.
Taking a conventional mortgage is acceptable if there's no Islamic alternative.
A sincere heart matters more to God than perfect observance of the rules.
Waiting for the Imam means working to change society now.
Majalis should be in English (or the local language), even if older members lose out.
If you're unsure whether something is halal, you avoid it.
The Quran is a book of guidance, not science, so it shouldn't be read for scientific facts.
A new ruling that breaks with centuries of opinion can still be correct.
Your faith has never seriously been shaken.
A majlis that doesn't connect Karbala to injustice today has missed the point.
You have no issue with taking out a loan for a mortgage.
You look up rulings (on wudu or khums, say) more often than you read about spirituality or ethics.
Until the Imam returns, believers should focus on their own piety rather than trying to change the world.
Keeping your family's language and customs at the centre is part of keeping the faith.
You'd eat at a restaurant without checking every ingredient, if the food is probably halal.
Science and religion answer different questions, so they can't truly conflict.
Someone can be close to God while being lax about some religious rules.
You feel most at home at a centre of people from your own background.
Matam is an essential part of mourning Imam Husayn, not just a cultural custom.
Many popular Shia practices are bid'ah: religious innovations with no basis in the Quran or the Imams' teaching.
